jlbind lets R packages call Julia code compiled ahead of time into a shared
library, without a Julia session. This vignette explains how that library works
and how to use an R package built with jlbind. To add Julia functions to your
own R package, see [Get started with jlbind](jlbind.html) and [Technical
details](technical-details.html). For how jlbind compares with other ways of
calling Julia from R, see
[Performance](https://bjarkehautop.github.io/jlbind/vignettes/articles/performance.html).

## How it works

An R process can load only one compiled Julia library. Julia has one runtime per
process, and that runtime uses a single compiled image. If two R packages loaded
separate copies of the library, they could conflict and crash the R session.

To avoid this, jlbind builds one shared library for each user, combining the
Julia code of all installed R packages that use jlbind (*clients*). When you run
`install_library()`, jlbind finds the installed clients, compiles their binding
packages into one library, and saves it under
`tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "data")`. Loading a client loads that library and
connects the client to it.

A client can only be bound to a library built from the version of that client
currently installed. If you update a package without rebuilding the library, its
functions will report that the library needs to be rebuilt.

## Using a package built on jlbind

You need [Julia](https://julialang.org/install/) 1.13 or later to build the
shared library.

After installing or updating an R package that uses jlbind, run:

```r
jlbind::install_library()
```

The first build downloads and compiles the required Julia dependencies, so it
may take a few minutes.

::: {.callout-note title="Restart R after rebuilding a library that is already loaded"}
Julia cannot be restarted within an R session. If the old library has already
been loaded, rebuilding it on disk does not replace the copy in memory. Restart
R to use the new library.
:::

### If something doesn't work correctly

If a package that uses jlbind doesn't work, first check its status:

```r
jlbind::check_bound("somepkg")
```

The most common causes are that the shared library hasn't been built yet, or
that the package was updated after the last build. For a full report, run:

```r
jlbind::jlbind_sitrep()
```

It shows the Julia that `install_library()` would use (with its version, and
whether it came from `JULIA` or the `PATH`), the library and what it was built
from, each installed package that uses jlbind and whether the library is current
for it, and the thread count. It works whether or not a library has loaded, and
returns the same information invisibly as a list.

If the Julia installation used for the build has been removed or replaced, for
example by a `juliaup` update, rebuild the library. `install_library()` rebuilds
it when the Julia version differs from the one it was built with. If the version
is the same, use `force = TRUE`:

```r
jlbind::install_library(force = TRUE)
```

You can select the Julia installation to use by setting the `JULIA` environment
variable or by passing `julia =` to `install_library()`.

The library is compiled for the building machine's CPU, and jlbind won't load it
on another. If one R library is used from computers with different CPUs, see
[Build options](#build-options).

### Threads

Julia runs with one thread by default. To use multiple threads, set
`JULIA_NUM_THREADS` before loading the first package that uses jlbind, for
example in your `.Renviron` file:

```sh
JULIA_NUM_THREADS=auto # or a number, such as 4
```

The thread count is fixed when the library is loaded, so restart R after
changing it.

### Dependency versions

All clients share a single set of Julia dependencies. By default, the build
starts from the versions in the `Manifest.toml` of the first client that has
one, and keeps them for the other clients where their `[compat]` bounds allow.
Pass `versions = "compat"` to ignore the manifests and let Julia's resolver
choose versions from the clients' `[compat]` bounds alone.

If a client's `[compat]` bounds conflict with those of the clients listed before
it by `jlbind_clients()`, it is left out of the build; `check_bound()` says
which clients it conflicts with.

You can control which clients are included by specifying them explicitly:

```r
jlbind::install_library(packages = c("pkgA", "pkgC"))
```

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Clients with incompatible dependencies cannot share a library"}
If you need both clients but never need them in the same R session, build a
separate library for each. Set `JLBIND_LIBRARY` before loading the client to
select the library for that session.

For example, build the two libraries:

```r
jlbind::build_library("pkgA", "~/jlbind/pkgA")
jlbind::build_library("pkgB", "~/jlbind/pkgB")
```

Then select one in an R session:

```r
# jlbind.dll on Windows, jlbind.dylib on macOS
Sys.setenv(JLBIND_LIBRARY = "~/jlbind/pkgA/jlbind.so")
library(pkgA)
```
:::

## Build options

jlbind compiles the library with these options, which keep it small and fast.
Most users don't need to change them.

  | Option                | What it does                       | How to change it                                                                                                                                                         |
  | --------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------                                                                                                                                                         |
  | `--output-lib`        | Builds a shared library            | Fixed                                                                                                                                                                    |
  | `--compile-ccallable` | Exports the clients' functions     | Fixed                                                                                                                                                                    |
  | `--trim=safe`         | Removes code that can't be reached | One client setting [`Config/jlbind/trim: false`](technical-details.html#compilation-constraints-trimming) turns it off for the whole library, which makes it much larger |
  | `--cpu-target=native` | Compiles for this computer's CPU   | `cpu_target` or `JULIA_CPU_TARGET`                                                                                                                                       |
  | `-g0`                 | Leaves out debug info              | `julia_args` or `JLBIND_JULIA_ARGS`                                                                                                                                      |

When trimming, JuliaC also passes `--experimental`, `--strip-ir` and
`--strip-metadata`.

### CPU target

Use `cpu_target` if one R library is used from computers with different CPUs,
such as cluster nodes sharing a home directory:

```r
jlbind::install_library(cpu_target = "generic")
```

This table compares the options on an x86-64 Linux computer (AMD Zen 4) with
Julia 1.14. Library size is the compiled library file for
[CausalStructures.jl](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/CausalStructures.jl), a
package of graph algorithms; the Julia runtime it loads adds about 6 MB. Run
times are relative to `"native"`, so 2× takes twice as long. Graph code is
CausalStructures.jl, and the other columns are small numeric kernels. Results
will differ for other packages and computers. The [benchmark
code](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/jlbind/tree/main/experiments/library-size)
is in the jlbind repository.

  | `cpu_target`                 | Runs on           | Library size | Graph code | SIMD loops | `exp`/`sin` |
  | --------------------         | ----------------- | -----------: | ---------: | ---------: | ----------: |
  | `"native"` (default)         | This CPU model    |       8.9 MB |         1× |         1× |          1× |
  | `"generic"`                  | Any CPU           |       8.8 MB |         1× |   1.7–2.8× |        1.1× |
  | Several targets              | The CPUs you list |        21 MB |   1.0–1.1× |   1.0–1.1× |        0.9× |
  | `"generic;native,clone_all"` | This CPU model    |      13.7 MB |         1× |         1× |        2.1× |

Sorting and a scalar ODE solver took about the same time with all of them.

The several targets measured here are those of Julia's own system image, which
keep numeric code fast across x86-64 CPUs:

```r
jlbind::install_library(
  cpu_target = paste(
    "generic",
    "sandybridge,-xsaveopt,clone_all",
    "haswell,-rdrnd,base(1)",
    "x86-64-v4,-rdrnd,base(1)",
    sep = ";"
  )
)
```

Build options count towards whether the library is up to date, so calling
`install_library()` without them rebuilds the library with the defaults. To keep
a target for every build, set `JULIA_CPU_TARGET`, for example in your
`.Renviron` file:

```sh
JULIA_CPU_TARGET=generic
```

### Julia arguments

For advanced use, `julia_args` passes extra options to Julia when it compiles
the library, such as `"-O3"`, or `"-g1"` to keep the debug info that jlbind
removes with `-g0`. You can also set them in `JLBIND_JULIA_ARGS`, separated by
spaces. They can't change the options jlbind relies on: `--trim`, `--output-*`
and `--compile-ccallable`.

### Libraries for people without Julia

The library loads the runtime of the Julia that built it, so that Julia must
stay installed. With `bundle = TRUE`, jlbind copies Julia's runtime next to the
library, using JuliaC's `--bundle`, so that it runs without Julia:

```r
jlbind::build_library(
  c("pkgA", "pkgB"),
  "~/jlbind/bundle",
  cpu_target = "generic",
  bundle = TRUE
)
```

Give them the whole directory, built on the same operating system and CPU
architecture as theirs. Then they should set `JLBIND_LIBRARY` to the library in
it before loading them.

The size depends on how much of the runtime you keep. Julia's whole runtime
includes libraries that many packages never use, such as OpenBLAS. These sizes
are for the whole directory, with `cpu_target = "generic"` on the computer
above, for CausalStructures.jl and for a tiny package:

  | Library                     | CausalStructures.jl | Tiny package |
  | --------------------------- | ------------------: | -----------: |
  | Not bundled (needs Julia)   |              8.8 MB |       2.0 MB |
  | Bundled                     |               87 MB |        68 MB |
  | Bundled and removed by hand |               15 MB |       8.9 MB |

To get the last row, delete `jlbind-bundle/share`, and everything in
`jlbind-bundle/lib` and `jlbind-bundle/lib/julia` except `libjulia`,
`libjulia-internal`, `libunwind`, `libz`, `libzstd`, `libatomic`, `libgcc_s` and
`libopenlibm`, then run `strip` on the library. jlbind doesn't do this for you,
because a package can need more of them; one using `LinearAlgebra` needs
OpenBLAS, for example. Test every package after removing anything.
